newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Troubled life of South Korea's "Crown Prince".
newsitem.headline: Troubled life of South Korea's "Crown Prince".

text.p: Once the brains behind his father's presidential campaigns, Kim Young-sam's jobless son, nicknamed the "Crown Prince", has for now become Kim's worst political liability.
Opposition politicians accuse Kim Hyun-chul, 38, of usurping the power of the presidency and filling his pockets through corrupt business dealings.
His own father apologised for his son's behaviour to placate public anger after Kim Hyun-chul was linked to a loans scandal involving a steelmaker that failed in January.
On Friday, he appeared in the National Assembly to be grilled by lawmakers over his role in the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co under debts of $5.8 billion.

Rarely seen in public, Kim Hyun-chul sought to correct his image as a wayward son in an autobiography published in 1995 called "Stories We Like to Tell, Stories We Like to Hear", a plea for understanding and sympathy.
It describes his anguished childhood when he was shadowed by security agents as the son of a persecuted opposition leader.
"I was proud of my father, who was a parliamentary member, but spent a gloomy adolesence watching my father walk through a life of thorn fields," he wrote.
His father was put under house arrest twice and hospitalised during a protest fast before he switched camps and joined the ruling party in 1990.
As an army conscript, Kim Hyun-chul was singled out for beatings. Job-hunting was a nightmare, despite a degree in business administration from the University of Southern California.
"It seemed like a normal working life was not going to be permitted to the opposition leader's son," he wrote.
An elder brother and three sisters left South Korea and settled in the United States.

Eventually, he landed a job at Ssangyong Securities, but only by lying about his father's name on the application form. He lasted just three months before quitting to help his father's campaign in the 1987 presidential elections.
Kim Young-sam was defeated and his son, now unemployed, set up a political research body with friends that plotted a victorious comeback race in 1992.
Allegations of corruption have dogged Kim ever since his father moved into the presidential Blue House mansion.
Newspapers tagged him the "Young Vice-President" and "Crown Prince", and editorials published only days after the elder Kim was sworn into office raised concerns about his son's influence-peddling.
Kim Hyun-chul and the Blue House fought back with legal threats. The Los Angeles Times and Le Monde, a French daily, were forced to run apologies over articles on the younger Kim.
The latest scandal concerns charges that Kim Hyun-chul took a 200-billion-won ($224-million) pay-off over an equipment purchase for bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co.
Opposition politicians allege the money was funneled to Kim by his best friend and colleague at the political research group, Park Tae-jung.
Ironically, it was his autobiography that first linked Kim to the scandal: 10,000 copies of the book were found in a warehouse of Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo.
Adding to his worries, an old friend and medical doctor, Park Kyung-shik, is out to take revenge over a soured business relationship.
Park has released a videotape taken by a closed-circuit camera at his urologist's clinic showing Kim Hyun-chul chatting on the telephone about a top media appointment.
He is not the first son of a South Korean president to make headlines.
The adopted son of South Korea's first president, the late Syngman Rhee, killed himself and his birth mother and father out of frustration with corruption.
And the troubled son of the late president Park Chung-hee has been arrested four times for drug offences and is serving a two-year suspended jail term.
